newsitem.title: USA: IBM warning rumor greeted with skepticism.
newsitem.headline: IBM warning rumor greeted with skepticism.

text.p: Rumors of an impending profit warning from International Business Machines Corp were greeted with skepticism by U.S. analysts, who saw little evidence of the kind of business weakness that would warrant such a move.
"I really have not heard anything that would suggest there's a catastrophe brewing," said Gery Helmig, an analyst at SoundView Financial.
Helmig also noted that IBM's one previous attempt at warning Wall Street about its prospects met with such disaster that the company may be shy of replicating the experience.
"IBM has only put out a profit warning once, in early 1993, and the stock really crumbled," he said.
Others on Wall Street concurred that unless some extraordinary development were behind it, a warning at this time seemed unlikely.
"I think the expectations on IBM are in a wide enough range that there shouldn't be a problem," said Joseph Battipaglia, chief investment officer at Gruntal & Co.
Brown Brothers Harriman analyst Bill Milton agreed, noting that estimates compiled by First Call for the fourth quarter earnings per share ranged from $3.13 to $4.32.
"I think it's a broad enough range to encompass all possibilities," Milton said.

One of the reasons IBM was particularly vulnerable to rumors, said analysts, is that the shares have staged a ferocious rally over the month and a half after several investment firms raised target prices on the company.
At their closing price of 157-3/4 on Tuesday, the shares have registered more than 30 points in gains from November 1, when they stood at 127-1/2.
With IBM chief executive Louis Gerstner in New York to deliver a speech at an Internet trade show, jitters apparently took hold of investors outside the U.S., where the rumors surfaced.
IBM declined to comment on the rumors and Gerstner's scheduled keynote address at the Internet World trade show concluded with no reference to earnings.
SoundView analyst Helmig said that had a significant problem arisen with earnings, it likely would have shown up in an area like mainframe demand, the personal computer business or exchange rates.
"Mainframe demand is certainly not slumping," he said. "The PC business I think is showing reasonably strong growth.
Foreign exchange rates have not shifted enough to warrant concern either, he said.
IBM shares were off 5/8 to 157-3/8 in early activity, well above their pre-opening lows.
